parsed.attack: The person who logs is never the person who benefits. Dictating thirty seconds after a hard phone call about your mother is friction paid now against a question somebody else might ask in March, and the one sibling who actually cares ends up doing all of it - which is the author's own first kill criterion, and the reason the cited caregiver tools churned despite validated need. Entry volume then collapses to the acute events only (a fall, a hospital visit, a contractor), which is one or two a quarter, under the stated floor of four a month by month three. And the whole thing has a hard terminal date: the log stops mattering the week the parent moves into care or dies, a median of two to three years out, at which point it becomes a file nobody opens.
parsed.strongest_defence: This is one of the few shapes where the state genuinely is worth defending - a year of dated entries on medications, contractors, payments and what the GP actually said is not reconstructible and not abandonable, and the crisis moment (a hospital admission, a probate argument between siblings) is precisely when a family discovers the record is the only thing standing between them and a fight. The trigger recurs for years without ever being scheduled, and unlike a notes file the log answers questions, which makes reading cheap enough that the second sibling joins to read before he ever writes.
parsed.verdict_reason: The accumulated record is real and genuinely defensible, but the act that creates it is unrewarded at the moment of doing it, which is the documented failure mode of every caregiver-logging product cited.
